papers.title: Selective deficiency of Atg7 attenuates radiation-induced neuronal injury via regulation of DRP1-mediated mitochondrial fission and FUNDC1-dependent mitophagy.
papers.summary: This study looks at how a protein called Atg7, which is essential for autophagy, affects neuron damage caused by radiation exposure. The researchers found that reducing Atg7 levels in specific neurons protected them from radiation injury by altering mitochondrial dynamics, specifically through DRP1-mediated mitochondrial fission and FUNDC1-dependent mitophagy. This suggests that too much autophagy/mitophagy can actually be harmful after radiation, and selectively limiting it may be neuroprotective.
papers.why: This paper provides direct mechanistic insight into mitophagy regulation via FUNDC1 and DRP1-mediated mitochondrial fission in neurons, which is central to understanding how disrupted mitochondrial quality control contributes to neuronal injury.

papers.title: LANCE-seq: Live-tissue Analysis via Needle-encoded Capture Extraction for Spatial Transcriptomics
papers.summary: LANCE-seq appears to be a new method that uses needle-based sampling to capture spatially-resolved transcriptomic information from live tissue. This likely allows researchers to extract RNA data tied to specific locations within intact, living tissue rather than relying solely on fixed sections. The approach could enable spatial transcriptomics in contexts where live-tissue sampling offers advantages over traditional slide-based methods.
papers.why: This method could offer a complementary or alternative spatial transcriptomics approach for profiling interneurons and perineuronal nets in brain tissue, potentially enabling live-tissue sampling to correlate with mitophagy/autophagy markers.

papers.summary: This paper offers a conceptual framework to help researchers plan spatial transcriptomics experiments more effectively from the outset. It likely covers key decisions such as choosing the right spatial resolution, tissue preparation strategies, and analytical pipelines appropriate to the biological question being asked. The goal is to help scientists avoid common pitfalls and better align their experimental design with their research goals before generating costly spatial data.

papers.title: Alleviation of Cuproptosis Contributes to the Reduction of Early Brain Injury by Mitophagy after Subarachnoid Hemorrhage.
papers.summary: This study investigates how subarachnoid hemorrhage (a type of brain bleed) causes early brain injury, focusing on a newly described form of cell death called cuproptosis, which is triggered by copper buildup. The researchers show that mitophagy, the process of clearing damaged mitochondria, can reduce cuproptosis and thereby lessen brain damage after the hemorrhage. The findings suggest that boosting mitophagy could be a therapeutic strategy to protect brain tissue following this type of stroke.
papers.why: This paper directly examines how mitophagy protects neurons from a novel metabolic/cell-death pathway (cuproptosis) tied to mitochondrial and copper metabolism, relevant to the project's focus on mitophagy's role in neuronal injury.
papers.figure: Figure showing mitophagy markers and cuproptosis-related protein levels (e.g., copper accumulation, DLAT, FDX1) in brain tissue after subarachnoid hemorrhage with and without mitophagy modulation.

papers.title: Transcriptomic identification of mitophagy-related plaque markers <i>HAND2</i>, <i>NRP1</i> and <i>RNF213</i>, with external replication and <i>in vivo</i> validation of <i>MLXIP</i>.
papers.summary: This study used transcriptomic analysis to find genes linked to mitophagy (the process of clearing damaged mitochondria) that are associated with atherosclerotic plaques, identifying HAND2, NRP1, and RNF213 as candidate markers. The findings were confirmed in an independent external dataset, and one gene, MLXIP, was further validated using in vivo experiments. This suggests these genes could serve as indicators of plaque-related mitochondrial quality control processes in cardiovascular disease.
papers.why: Although focused on vascular plaques rather than brain tissue, the transcriptomic approach to identifying mitophagy-related markers and validating them in vivo offers methodological parallels relevant to studying mitophagy signatures in neuronal spatial transcriptomics datasets.

papers.title: CIRCA learns identifiable cell- and niche-level programs and their interactions with tissue pathology from spatial transcriptomics
papers.summary: CIRCA is a new computational method designed to analyze spatial transcriptomics data by identifying distinct molecular programs operating at both the individual cell level and the broader tissue niche level. It aims to make these learned programs 'identifiable,' meaning they are statistically robust and interpretable rather than arbitrary mathematical artifacts. The tool also links these programs to tissue pathology, helping researchers understand how specific cellular and niche-level gene expression patterns relate to disease states.
papers.why: This computational framework could help disentangle how spatial gene expression programs in specific niches, such as those surrounding interneurons and perineuronal nets, relate to pathology, offering a method applicable to spatial transcriptomics data in mitophagy/autophagy studies.

papers.title: Autophagy induction by cytoplasmic Acinus requires Lrrk activity
papers.summary: This study investigates how the protein Acinus, when located in the cytoplasm, triggers autophagy, the cell's process for degrading and recycling damaged components. The researchers found that this autophagy-inducing function of Acinus depends on the activity of Lrrk, a kinase enzyme best known for its link to Parkinson's disease. The work provides mechanistic insight into a new pathway controlling autophagy initiation at the molecular level.
papers.why: Since Lrrk is a Parkinson's-associated kinase and autophagy/mitophagy dysfunction is central to neurodegeneration, this mechanistic link could inform mitophagy and autophagy regulation in neurons relevant to the PhD project's core focus.

papers.title: Exercise-conditioned serum drives mitochondrial remodeling in neurons.
papers.summary: This study looks at how serum collected from exercised animals or people affects neurons when applied in culture or in vivo. The researchers appear to find that exercise-conditioned serum triggers changes in neuronal mitochondrial structure or function, suggesting a blood-borne signal links physical activity to brain cell metabolism. This points to a systemic mechanism by which exercise could influence neuronal health via mitochondrial remodeling.
papers.why: Since mitophagy and mitochondrial quality control in neurons are central to this PhD project, evidence that exercise-conditioned serum induces mitochondrial remodeling in neurons could reveal a novel upstream physiological trigger worth testing with spatial transcriptomic or metabolomic readouts in interneuron populations.
